dart2js compile time vs. generated code shape

2026-10-02T06:16:52.195927 · Dart 3.13.5 · macos Version 27.0.1 (Build 26A434) · 10 cores · 259 compiles, N = 1 to 4000

Each point is a single dart compile js -O3 --csp of a generated program with N classes, all instantiated in one main. Variants change one aspect of the generated code; see variants in gen.dart.

Comparing variants: Synthetic ZBase_i classes

Each ZBase_i has an int field plus some combination of ==, hashCode and toString overrides.

  • The parameter type of == matters: == (Object other) is fastest at 26.6s and == (dynamic other) slowest at 28.7s (7.9% slower) at N=4000.
  • Overriding == costs 5.10s (1.2×) at N=4000 (== (dynamic other) at 28.7s vs. no == override at 23.6s). The biggest difference is in Enqueue (2.35s, 46% of it), mostly resolution.dynamicUse (2.06s). Scaling goes from N2.12 to N1.99.
  • Adding a hashCode override to a toString override costs 2.45s (1.1×) at N=4000 (no == override at 23.6s vs. toString only at 21.1s). The biggest difference is in SSA builder (833ms, 34% of it). Scaling goes from N2.29 to N2.12.
  • Adding a toString override to a hashCode override costs 2.30s (1.1×) at N=4000 (no == override at 23.6s vs. hashCode only at 21.3s). The biggest difference is in kernel loader (525ms, 23% of it). Scaling goes from N2.11 to N2.12.
  • Reading the shared field val inside toString costs 16.6s (4.6×) at N=4000 (toString only at 21.1s vs. toString only, no field read at 4.55s). The biggest difference is in Enqueue (11.8s, 71% of it), mostly resolution.dynamicUse (11.8s). Scaling goes from N1.39 to N2.29.
  • A toString override that does not read any field costs 1.24s (1.4×) at N=4000 (toString only, no field read at 4.55s vs. no overrides at 3.31s). The biggest difference is in Code emitter (325ms, 26% of it). Scaling goes from N1.34 to N1.39.
  • Every class declaring a field with the same name (vs. unique names) costs 16.5s (2.4×) at N=4000 (== (dynamic other) at 28.7s vs. == (dynamic other), unique field names at 12.2s). The biggest difference is in Enqueue (13.4s, 81% of it), mostly resolution.dynamicUse (13.3s). Scaling goes from N1.58 to N1.99.
  • Declaring val on every subclass (vs. once on the base class) costs 17.3s (2.5×) at N=4000 (== (dynamic other) at 28.7s vs. == (dynamic other), field on base class at 11.4s). The biggest difference is in Enqueue (13.4s, 77% of it), mostly resolution.dynamicUse (13.3s). Scaling goes from N1.51 to N1.99.
  • All N inserts in one giant main (vs. helpers of 100 statements) costs 12.6s (1.8×) at N=4000 (== (dynamic other) at 28.7s vs. == (dynamic other), main split up at 16.0s). The biggest difference is in Enqueue (13.1s, 104% of it), mostly resolution.dynamicUse (13.1s). Scaling goes from N1.83 to N1.99.
  • A giant main once field names are unique makes little difference at N=4000 (== (dynamic other), unique field names at 12.2s vs. unique field names + main split up at 12.5s). Scaling goes from N1.60 to N1.58.
  • All classes in one library (vs. a library per class, same public field name) saves 11.6s (1.4×) at N=4000 (== (dynamic other) at 28.7s vs. == (dynamic other), library per class at 40.3s). The biggest difference is in Enqueue (6.65s, 57% of it), mostly resolution.dynamicUse (6.39s). Scaling goes from N2.04 to N1.99.
  • A public field name shared across libraries (vs. a private _val per library) costs 14.9s (1.6×) at N=4000 (== (dynamic other), library per class at 40.3s vs. == (dynamic other), library per class, private _val at 25.4s). The biggest difference is in Enqueue (15.3s, 103% of it), mostly resolution.dynamicUse (15.4s). Scaling goes from N1.48 to N2.04.

Comparing variants: Frugal-style structs

Each N adds one struct shaped like Frugal’s generated Dart (six fields whose names id, name, description, count, tags and child are shared by every struct; child is the previous struct), in its own library, plus a service client calling through FMethod. So N=1000 is 2000 classes. The variants apply the generator changes recommended in research/frugal-dart-codegen.md. These stop at N=1000 because they are much slower to compile.

  • Generated internals going through the shared public getters, isSetX() and validate() (vs. private fields and _validate()) costs 10.1s (1.4×) at N=1000 (Frugal-style, as generated today at 35.5s vs. Frugal-style, internals use private fields and _validate() at 25.5s). The biggest difference is in SSA builder (4.65s, 46% of it). Scaling goes from N1.11 to N1.23.
  • FMethod calling Function.apply on a tear-off (vs. a typed closure) saves 3.95s (1.1×) at N=1000 (Frugal-style, as generated today at 35.5s vs. Frugal-style, FMethod without Function.apply at 39.5s). The biggest difference is in Enqueue (1.83s, 46% of it), mostly resolution.dynamicUse (1.86s). Scaling goes from N1.29 to N1.23.
  • static final descriptors, implicit dynamic return types and a new DeepCollectionEquality per call (vs. const, explicit types and a shared instance) costs 2.49s (1.1×) at N=1000 (Frugal-style, as generated today at 35.5s vs. Frugal-style, const descriptors and explicit return types at 33.0s). The biggest difference is in Enqueue (689ms, 28% of it), mostly resolution.dynamicUse (539ms). Scaling goes from N1.24 to N1.23.
  • Generating getFieldValue, setFieldValue, isSet, clone and toString (vs. a lean mode without them) costs 11.9s (1.5×) at N=1000 (Frugal-style, as generated today at 35.5s vs. Frugal-style, no getFieldValue/setFieldValue/isSet/clone/toString at 23.7s). The biggest difference is in SSA builder (3.67s, 31% of it). Scaling goes from N1.23 to N1.23.
  • Inline list loops in read/write (vs. shared runtime helpers) makes little difference at N=1000 (Frugal-style, as generated today at 35.5s vs. Frugal-style, shared list read/write helpers at 35.2s). Scaling goes from N1.21 to N1.23.
  • Frugal output as generated today (vs. all recommended changes together) costs 15.3s (1.8×) at N=1000 (Frugal-style, as generated today at 35.5s vs. Frugal-style, all of the above at 20.2s). The biggest difference is in SSA builder (5.07s, 33% of it). Scaling goes from N1.20 to N1.23.

Breakdown for hashCode only

  • Compile time went from 334ms at N=1 to 21.3s at N=4000, 64× slower for 4000× more classes. From N=1000 up it scales as roughly N2.11 (about quadratic).
  • Most of the extra time comes from Enqueue (+11.4s, 54% of the increase), SSA builder (+4.07s, 19% of the increase) and SSA optimizer (+1.94s, 9.3% of the increase).
  • Fastest-growing phases that take at least 5% of the time at N=4000: Enqueue > resolution.dynamicUse (N2.94, 52% of the time), Enqueue (N2.86, 54% of the time) and SSA optimizer > SsaLoadElimination (N2.32, 5.3% of the time). These grow faster than the total, so they will dominate even more at larger N.
  • Between N=100 and N=4000, Enqueue grew from 4.4% to 54% of compile time, while kernel loader fell from 34% to 5.4%.
  • The amount of work dart2js reports grows at most as N0.93 (about 16 inferred types per class), but time grows as N2.11. The cost per element is rising with program size, which points at non-linear behavior inside the phases above rather than just more code to compile.
  • Outside the compiler itself (VM startup, make), each compile costs a roughly fixed 116ms of wall-clock time on average.

Breakdown for == (dynamic other), main split up

  • Compile time went from 347ms at N=1 to 16.0s at N=4000, 46× slower for 4000× more classes. From N=1000 up it scales as roughly N1.83 (about quadratic).
  • Most of the extra time comes from SSA builder (+5.04s, 32% of the increase), SSA optimizer (+2.89s, 18% of the increase) and kernel loader (+1.86s, 12% of the increase).
  • Fastest-growing phases that take at least 5% of the time at N=4000: SSA optimizer > SsaLoadElimination (N2.52, 7.6% of the time), SSA builder (N2.30, 32% of the time) and SSA optimizer (N1.98, 18% of the time). These grow faster than the total, so they will dominate even more at larger N.
  • Between N=100 and N=4000, SSA builder grew from 10% to 32% of compile time, while kernel loader fell from 35% to 13%.
  • The amount of work dart2js reports grows at most as N0.96 (about 43 inferred types per class), but time grows as N1.83. The cost per element is rising with program size, which points at non-linear behavior inside the phases above rather than just more code to compile.
  • Outside the compiler itself (VM startup, make), each compile costs a roughly fixed 115ms of wall-clock time on average.

Breakdown for == (dynamic other), library per class

  • Compile time went from 348ms at N=1 to 40.3s at N=4000, 116× slower for 4000× more classes. From N=1000 up it scales as roughly N2.04 (about quadratic).
  • Most of the extra time comes from Enqueue (+20.7s, 52% of the increase), kernel loader (+5.01s, 13% of the increase) and SSA builder (+4.34s, 11% of the increase).
  • Fastest-growing phases that take at least 5% of the time at N=4000: Enqueue > resolution.dynamicUse (N3.16, 49% of the time), Enqueue (N2.99, 51% of the time) and SSA optimizer > SsaLoadElimination (N2.74, 5.3% of the time). These grow faster than the total, so they will dominate even more at larger N.
  • Between N=100 and N=4000, Enqueue grew from 3.7% to 51% of compile time, while kernel loader fell from 40% to 13%.
  • The amount of work dart2js reports grows at most as N0.96 (about 41 inferred types per class), but time grows as N2.04. The cost per element is rising with program size, which points at non-linear behavior inside the phases above rather than just more code to compile.
  • Outside the compiler itself (VM startup, make), each compile costs a roughly fixed 139ms of wall-clock time on average.

Breakdown for Frugal-style, shared list read/write helpers

  • Compile time went from 479ms at N=1 to 35.2s at N=1000, 73× slower for 1000× more classes. From N=250 up it scales as roughly N1.21 (superlinear).
  • Most of the extra time comes from SSA builder (+9.25s, 27% of the increase), Enqueue (+7.93s, 23% of the increase) and Type inference (+3.93s, 11% of the increase).
  • Fastest-growing phases that take at least 5% of the time at N=1000: Enqueue > resolution.dynamicUse (N2.13, 19% of the time), Enqueue (N1.90, 23% of the time) and SSA builder (N1.37, 26% of the time). These grow faster than the total, so they will dominate even more at larger N.
  • Between N=100 and N=1000, Enqueue grew from 5.3% to 23% of compile time, while kernel loader fell from 18% to 9.3%.
  • The amount of work dart2js reports grows at most as N0.97 (about 1156 inferred types per class), but time grows as N1.21. The cost per element is rising with program size, which points at non-linear behavior inside the phases above rather than just more code to compile.
  • Outside the compiler itself (VM startup, make), each compile costs a roughly fixed 97ms of wall-clock time on average.

  • Compile time went from 434ms at N=1 to 20.2s at N=1000, 47× slower for 1000× more classes. From N=250 up it scales as roughly N1.20 (superlinear).
  • Most of the extra time comes from SSA builder (+4.33s, 22% of the increase), SSA optimizer (+2.86s, 14% of the increase) and Enqueue (+2.71s, 14% of the increase).
  • Fastest-growing phases that take at least 5% of the time at N=1000: Enqueue > resolution.dynamicUse (N1.96, 9.3% of the time), Enqueue (N1.70, 14% of the time) and SSA builder (N1.46, 22% of the time). These grow faster than the total, so they will dominate even more at larger N.
  • Between N=100 and N=1000, SSA builder grew from 13% to 22% of compile time, while kernel loader fell from 22% to 12%.
  • The amount of work dart2js reports grows at most as N0.96 (about 639 inferred types per class), but time grows as N1.20. The cost per element is rising with program size, which points at non-linear behavior inside the phases above rather than just more code to compile.
  • Outside the compiler itself (VM startup, make), each compile costs a roughly fixed 93ms of wall-clock time on average.
